ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Letting a correction policy revise its own earlier relabelling decisions
PROPOSAL: We train a label-correction agent that visits every training sample once per epoch and may keep, change or restore its label, so a correction made early can be undone once the classifier has learned more, in contrast with policies that commit once. The agent sees the sample's features, its current and original labels and the classifier's predictive distribution, and receives as reward the change in accuracy on a small trusted split over the following epoch. We run it on image benchmarks with instance-dependent noise at severe rates and report clean test accuracy and the precision and recall of the final labels against the true ones, together with the number of reversals made in each epoch.
CONTROLS: A comparison with the same agent allowed a single decision per sample at matched decisions per epoch and with greedy correction by the classifier's own predictions, a reference run with clean labels, the same setting repeated with the trusted split varied in size, and final label precision measured against the true labels at every epoch, over five seeds.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: The revising agent should end with higher clean accuracy and higher label precision than the commit-once agent, with most reversals happening in the middle of training. A null result is a precision curve that the commit-once agent matches at every epoch, or reversals that are as often wrong as right.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A label-correction agent that may undo earlier changes
PROPOSAL: We design a correction agent that passes over the whole training set each epoch and can keep, change or restore every label, so that an early change is reversible once the classifier has moved on, unlike agents that decide once and stop. Its inputs are the sample's features, the current and original labels and the classifier's predictive distribution, and its reward is the change in accuracy on a small trusted split across the next epoch. Experiments use image benchmarks with instance-dependent noise at severe rates, and we follow the agent's return, the training loss on the current labels and the number of labels changed and restored per epoch.
CONTROLS: A comparison with the same agent allowed a single decision per sample at matched decisions per epoch and with greedy correction by the classifier's own predictions, a reference run with clean labels, the same setting repeated with the trusted split varied in size, and the agent's return measured against the training loss on the current labels at every epoch, over five seeds.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: The revising agent should reach a higher return and a lower training loss than the commit-once agent, with most reversals happening in the middle of training. A null result is a return curve that the commit-once agent matches at every epoch, or reversals that are as often wrong as right.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploration guided by feature neighbours for instance-dependent label noise
PROPOSAL: Because instance-dependent noise flips labels toward classes that look alike in feature space, we give a stochastic correction policy an exploration bonus for trying, on a suspected sample, the labels held by its nearest neighbours in a pretrained feature space, and we decay the bonus as those labels are tried. The policy is rewarded by the accuracy change on a trusted split over the next epoch. We test on image benchmarks with instance-dependent noise built from feature similarity at rates up to half the labels, where the confusable classes are exactly the neighbours, and report clean accuracy and correction precision.
CONTROLS: A comparison with a uniform exploration bonus over all classes at matched exploration rate and with the policy without any bonus, a reference run with greedy correction by the classifier's predictions, the same setting repeated with class-conditional noise at the same rates for contrast, and correction precision measured against the true labels in the confusable class pairs, over five seeds.
COST: 290
PREDICTION: The neighbour bonus should lift precision in confusable pairs beyond the uniform bonus at severe instance-dependent rates, and the two bonuses should tie under class-conditional noise. The idea is refuted if the uniform bonus matches it under instance-dependent noise, or if precision in confusable pairs does not move.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A neighbour-based exploration bonus for stochastic label correction
PROPOSAL: We add to a stochastic correction policy an exploration bonus that favours, for a suspected sample, the labels carried by its nearest neighbours in a pretrained feature space, decaying the bonus as each candidate is tried, on the reasoning that neighbouring labels are the most likely alternatives when a label is wrong. The reward is the change in trusted-split accuracy over the next epoch. We evaluate on image benchmarks with symmetric class-conditional noise at mild rates, where every class is as likely as any other as a flip target, so that the bonus can be read in a clean and well understood regime, reporting clean accuracy and correction precision.
CONTROLS: A comparison with a uniform exploration bonus over all classes at matched exploration rate and with the policy without any bonus, a reference run with greedy correction by the classifier's predictions, the same setting repeated with symmetric noise at milder rates for contrast, and correction precision measured against the true labels in the most frequent class pairs, over five seeds.
COST: 290
PREDICTION: The neighbour bonus should lift precision in the most frequent class pairs beyond the uniform bonus at mild symmetric rates, and the two bonuses should tie at the mildest rate. The idea is refuted if the uniform bonus matches it at every symmetric rate, or if precision in frequent pairs does not move.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Does a correction policy need the training history of each sample
PROPOSAL: We compare a correction policy that reads, for each sample, the sequence of its losses, predicted classes and confidences over all past epochs through a small recurrent network, with a policy that reads only the current epoch's values, both trained with the same delayed reward from a trusted split. The hypothesis is that long-term decisions need the trajectory, since samples that were learned late and forgotten often carry wrong labels. Both policies run on image benchmarks with instance-dependent noise at high rates, and we record clean test accuracy, correction precision and the epochs at which corrections occur, splitting every metric between samples learned early and samples learned late.
CONTROLS: A comparison with the history-free policy at matched parameter count and with a policy given the history truncated to the last few epochs, a reference run with greedy correction from the current prediction, the same setting repeated with the history length varied from one epoch to all of them, and correction precision measured against the true labels for samples learned late, over five seeds.
COST: 170
PREDICTION: The full-history policy should gain most on samples learned late and lose little on samples learned early, with precision rising with history length up to the full trajectory. The hypothesis is contradicted if the truncated history matches the full one, or if precision on late-learned samples stays flat across lengths.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A recurrent correction policy that reads each sample's loss trajectory
PROPOSAL: We build a correction policy whose input, for each training sample, is the sequence of losses, predicted classes and confidences recorded at every past epoch, encoded by a small recurrent network, and we train it with a delayed reward from a trusted split, on the view that samples learned late and then forgotten tend to carry wrong labels and are best spotted from their trajectory. The policy runs on image benchmarks with instance-dependent noise at high rates, and we examine how its clean test accuracy, correction precision and timing of corrections respond to the augmentation applied to the images, the optimiser of the classifier and the image side used in training.
CONTROLS: A comparison with the history policy under a stronger data augmentation at matched parameter count and with the policy under a second optimiser for the classifier, a reference run with greedy correction from the current prediction, the same setting repeated with the image side varied from small to full size, and correction precision measured against the true labels for samples of each augmentation, over five seeds.
COST: 170
PREDICTION: The recurrent policy should keep its precision under stronger augmentation and under either optimiser, with corrections concentrated in the middle epochs. The hypothesis is contradicted if precision changes with the optimiser, or if corrections spread evenly across epochs under every augmentation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Planning label corrections with short simulated training rollouts
PROPOSAL: Before committing to a label change, the corrector simulates a few gradient steps of a small proxy classifier under each candidate label for a group of suspected samples and scores each candidate by the simulated change in accuracy on a trusted split, choosing the candidate with the best estimated effect. This gives a model-based way to weigh consequences without waiting for the real training to reveal them. We test on image benchmarks with instance-dependent noise at high rates, reporting clean test accuracy, correction precision and the wall-clock overhead of the rollouts relative to the main training, for proxy classifiers of several widths.
CONTROLS: A comparison with greedy correction by the classifier's predictions on the same backbone at matched correction rate and with a learned policy trained from delayed rewards on the same backbone, a reference run with clean labels on the same backbone, the same setting repeated with the rollout length varied from one step to a full epoch, and correction precision measured against the true labels, over five seeds.
COST: 390
PREDICTION: Rollout planning should gain over greedy correction at the highest noise rates and come close to the delayed-reward policy at lower overhead for every proxy width. The approach is disproved if greedy correction on the same backbone matches it at every rate, or if gains vanish for the shortest rollouts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Model-based label correction through proxy-classifier rollouts
PROPOSAL: For each group of suspected samples the corrector runs a few gradient steps of a small proxy classifier under every candidate label, reads the change in accuracy on a trusted split that each candidate produces in simulation, and commits to the candidate with the highest estimated gain, so that consequences are weighed before the main training sees the new label. We study the method on image benchmarks with instance-dependent noise at high rates, recording clean test accuracy, correction precision and the time spent in rollouts, and we place its results beside those of smaller and larger backbones trained with other correction rules.
CONTROLS: A comparison with greedy correction by the classifier's predictions on a smaller backbone at matched correction rate and with a learned policy trained from delayed rewards on a wider backbone, a reference run with clean labels on a larger backbone, the same setting repeated with the rollout length varied from one step to a full epoch, and correction precision measured against the true labels, over five seeds.
COST: 390
PREDICTION: Rollout planning should gain over greedy correction on the smaller backbone at the highest noise rates and come close to the wider-backbone policy at lower overhead. The approach is disproved if greedy correction on the smaller backbone matches it at every rate, or if gains vanish for the shortest rollouts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training a correction agent against an adversary that crafts instance-dependent noise
PROPOSAL: We pair a learned label-correction agent with an adversary that, given a sample's features, chooses which label to corrupt it to and how often, within a rate limit, so as to lower the agent's downstream accuracy, and we train both in alternation on image benchmarks. The aim is a corrector that stays effective in complex and highly noisy scenarios it has not seen. After training, the corrector is evaluated on held-out noise patterns: feature-similarity noise, noise from a different pretrained feature space and real annotation noise, reporting clean test accuracy and correction precision.
CONTROLS: A comparison with the same corrector trained on the target noise pattern directly at matched training steps and with the corrector trained on symmetric noise only, a reference run with greedy correction by the classifier's predictions, the same setting repeated with the adversary's rate limit varied, and correction precision measured against the true labels on each held-out pattern, over five seeds.
COST: 470
PREDICTION: The adversarially trained corrector should approach the corrector trained on the target pattern and clearly pass the symmetric-noise corrector on every held-out pattern. The result counts as negative if the symmetric-noise corrector matches it on real annotation noise, or if the corrector trained on the target pattern stays far ahead everywhere.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial noise generation for robust learned label correction
PROPOSAL: A learned correction agent is trained in alternation with an adversary that reads a sample's features and picks, under a rate limit, the class its label is flipped to and how often, with the goal of pulling the agent's downstream accuracy down, on image benchmarks with their original labels taken as clean. The intent is a corrector that keeps working under difficult noise it has never met. We evaluate the trained corrector on held-out patterns, feature-similarity noise, noise drawn from a second pretrained feature space and real annotation noise, and we examine how its clean test accuracy and correction precision depend on the adversary's architecture and training length.
CONTROLS: A comparison with the same corrector trained against an adversary of a wider architecture at matched training steps and with the corrector trained against the adversary for twice as long, a reference run with greedy correction by the classifier's predictions, the same setting repeated with the adversary's rate limit varied, and correction precision measured against the labels chosen by the adversary on each held-out pattern, over five seeds.
COST: 470
PREDICTION: The adversarially trained corrector should reach similar accuracy whatever the adversary's width and clearly gain from longer adversarial training on every held-out pattern. The result counts as negative if the wider adversary gives a different corrector on real annotation noise, or if longer training leaves the corrector far behind everywhere.
